Goals: Explain why squaring each side of an equation, or taking the square root of each side, may result in an inequivalent equation.
Use graphs to represent solutions to equations involving squares and square roots.

SourceElements.SourceSection: 7.5: Solve These Equations With Square Roots in Them
SourceElements.SourceExcerpt: Every positive number has two square roots. You can see this by looking at the graph of \(y=x^2\):

SourceElements.SourceSection: 7.5: Solve These Equations With Square Roots in Them
SourceElements.SourceExcerpt: If \(y\) is a positive number like 4, then we can see that \(y=4\) crosses the graph in two places, so the equation \(x^2=4\) will have two solutions, namely, \(\sqrt{4}\) and \(\text{-}\sqrt{4}\). This is true for any positive number…

SourceElements.SourceSection: 7.5: Solve These Equations With Square Roots in Them
SourceElements.SourceExcerpt: When we have a square root in an equation like \(\sqrt{t} - 6 = 0\), we can isolate the square root and then square each side:

SourceElements.SourceSection: 7.5: Solve These Equations With Square Roots in Them
SourceElements.SourceExcerpt: \(\begin{align}\sqrt{t} - 6 &= 0\\ \sqrt{t} &= 6\\ t &= 6^2 \\ t &= 36 \end{align}\)

SourceElements.SourceSection: 7.5: Solve These Equations With Square Roots in Them
SourceElements.SourceExcerpt: But sometimes, squaring each side of an equation gives results that aren’t solutions to the original equation. For example:

SourceElements.SourceSection: 7.5: Solve These Equations With Square Roots in Them
SourceElements.SourceExcerpt: \(\begin{align}\sqrt{t} + 6 &= 0\\ \sqrt{t} &= \text-6\\ t &= (\text-6)^2 \\ t &= 36 \end{align}\)

SourceElements.SourceSection: 7.5: Solve These Equations With Square Roots in Them
SourceElements.SourceExcerpt: Note that 36 is not a solution to the original equation, because \(\sqrt{36}+6\) doesn’t equal 0. In fact, \(\sqrt{t}+6=0\) has no solutions, because it’s impossible for the sum of two positive numbers to be zero.

SourceElements.SourceSection: 7.5: Solve These Equations With Square Roots in Them
SourceElements.SourceExcerpt: Remember: sometimes the new equation has solutions that the old equation doesn’t have. Always check your solutions in the original equation!
